# CasaVargas, full facts

> Casa Vargas LLC is an independent software studio in North Carolina, founded by Jon Vargas. It makes apps for the Mac, iPhone, iPad, Apple TV, Windows and Linux, sold as one-time purchases or free, with no subscriptions.

This file gives the fuller per-product facts behind the summary in /llms.txt: what each product does, why it exists, how it's built, and its pricing. Each product's own site is the source of truth for prices and features; this file and the case studies it is drawn from are kept in sync with those sites.

## Beltr

Product site: https://beltr.app | Case study: https://casavargas.app/work/beltr/

Beltr is living-room karaoke built on your own music library. It removes the vocals from songs you already own, times the lyrics to them word by word, and puts them on the TV while guests join from their phones. All of the processing runs on your own computer or home server. Runs on macOS, Windows, Linux and Docker (home server). Price: $19.99 once; five songs are free to try, no card needed.

Why it exists: home karaoke has mostly become a subscription, a licensed catalog rented by the year and limited to whatever it carries this month. Beltr starts from the other end: your library is the catalog and your own hardware does the work, so there is nothing to rent.

What it does:
- Your music folder is the catalog. Point Beltr at a folder or an Apple Music library and every MP3, FLAC and WAV appears, searchable by artist, album and genre. Nothing is copied or moved.
- Vocal separation on your machine. On-device AI splits each song into vocals and instrumental in a minute or two. Nothing is uploaded.
- Lyrics timed word by word. Lyrics come from LRCLIB or your own paste and are aligned to the vocal track. When none exist, a local speech model drafts them first.
- Phones join with a QR code. Guests queue songs, control playback and sing from their phones, with live pitch scoring. There is no app or account to set up.
- Plays and exports karaoke files. CDG, MP3+G, .kar, .mid and Thai NCN files play with lyrics read straight from the file, and songs export to MP3+G, CDG or .kar for hardware machines.
- Runs on a home server too. The same engine ships as a Docker image for Unraid and other home servers, in CPU, NVIDIA and Intel GPU builds.

How it's built: one inference runtime (ONNX Runtime, no PyTorch), one WebSocket room protocol shared by the TV page, web remote and four native apps, bounded-memory separation that can offload to a faster machine on the network, old karaoke formats rendered into the same pipeline as separated songs, and one tagged release building signed and notarized macOS, Windows (including a Microsoft Store package), Linux and container builds.

On the record: 83 public desktop releases between May 21 and September 24, 2026. About 800 test files across Python, JavaScript and Playwright. A desktop app, four native companion apps and three container builds.

Companion apps: Beltr Remote (iPhone, Android) and Beltr Client (Apple TV, Android TV), both free.

## OneScribe

Product site: https://getonescribe.app | Case study: https://casavargas.app/work/onescribe/ | App Store: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/onescribe-ai-note-scanner/id6756506734

OneScribe turns a photo of a receipt, a lease or a boarding pass into a structured card: the vendor, the dates, the amounts, the deadlines. The reading happens on the device; there's no account to create and no OneScribe server to send anything to. Runs on iOS 26 and iPadOS 26. Price: free to scan; Pro is $9.99 once.

Why it exists: most scans end up as a flat image or a block of text, so the information people actually need, like when a warranty ends or what a lease says about notice, stays buried. Many of these documents are also among the most private a person owns (tax forms, prescriptions, IDs), which made on-device processing the starting point, not a feature.

What it does:
- A card for every document. OneScribe knows dozens of kinds of document, each with its own Data Card. A receipt card holds the line items, tax and total; a contract card holds the deadlines and renewal windows.
- Ask in plain English. Search the whole library in natural language, or chat with a single document. Voice conversations run on the device too.
- A daily briefing. Each morning it lists what needs attention, from upcoming deadlines to recent spending.
- Alerts before deadlines. You hear about it before a warranty lapses, a return window closes or a policy comes up for renewal.
- Documents that link up. Related documents connect automatically: a receipt with its warranty, an invoice with its payment, an insurance card with a vehicle registration.
- Exports to the right app. Contracts go to Calendar, business cards to Contacts, meeting notes to Reminders and receipts to a spreadsheet.

How it's built: every document type is a Swift `@Generable` struct, so Apple's on-device model fills typed fields instead of writing prose. There are 151 schemas and about 1,420 field instructions, all written in one house style. After each extraction a validator flags impossible dates, negative amounts and balances that don't add up. A single Vision document request per page returns text in reading order with structure and barcodes; a Core ML classifier identifies the document type first and only sends ambiguous documents to the language model. Document links come from a pure rule engine, and the daily briefing is built from rules, with the model only writing the headline and first paragraph.

On the record: 19 export modes. 151 typed schemas, with about 1,420 field instructions. On the App Store since January 2026.

## DebridDownloader (open source)

Repo: https://github.com/CasaVargas/DebridDownloader | Case study: https://casavargas.app/work/debrid-downloader/

DebridDownloader is a free, open-source desktop app for people who pay for Real-Debrid, TorBox or Premiumize. It replaces the browser tab: you add a link or a file, the service fetches it, and you download, stream or file the results without leaving the app. Runs on macOS (Apple Silicon only), Windows and Linux. Built with Tauri, Rust and React. License: GPL-3.0. Free; requires an account with one of the three services.

Why it exists: debrid services are run from a web dashboard, where you add a link, wait, then click through file links one at a time while the browser saves each one. There is no queue to control, nothing files finished downloads where a media server expects them, and API tokens tend to end up pasted into scripts and extensions. DebridDownloader moves that workflow into a native app and keeps credentials in the operating system's keychain.

What it does:
- Three services in one app. Connect Real-Debrid (with OAuth or a token), TorBox or Premiumize, and switch between them at any time.
- A queue you control. Run one to ten downloads at once, with live speed and time remaining, an optional speed limit and a notification when each one finishes.
- Stream before you download. Preview a video straight from your provider in a floating mini-player, without saving it first.
- Files land where your library looks. Sort downloads into movie and TV folders using TMDB, trigger a library scan in Plex, Jellyfin or Emby, or send files to an rclone remote.
- Handles links from the system. Set it as the default handler and new links add themselves. It stays in the tray and can start at login.
- Keyboard first, secrets in the keychain. Command-K to search, arrow keys to move, Return to download. Tokens live in Keychain, Credential Manager or Secret Service, never in a settings file.

How it's built: a Rust async trait defines about a dozen operations, and each provider's client translates its own API into shared types; the active provider can be swapped at runtime, and commands clone it and release the lock before awaiting so a slow network call never blocks a switch. A Tokio semaphore caps how many downloads run at once, each streaming to disk with its own cancellation handle, with progress reaching the React front end as events at most every 100 ms and one speed limiter covering both local and rclone destinations. A local Axum server on a random localhost port serves one URL per preview session and forwards range requests so the player can seek inside a remote file. Links arrive three ways, the system deep link, a hand-off from a second instance, and command-line arguments on a cold start, and all three pass the same validator before anything reaches a provider. A GitHub Actions matrix builds five targets from one workflow: macOS on Apple Silicon, Windows on x64 and ARM64, and Linux on x64 and ARM64, with signed and notarized macOS builds and signed update bundles; because Tauri uses the system web view, the installers stay under 9 MB.

On the record: GPL-3.0 licensed. 16 releases, from version 1.0 in March 2026 to 1.6.4 in May 2026. Installer size 5.9 MB on Windows, 8.9 MB on macOS. Open to pull requests; version 1.6.4 included seven from an outside contributor.

## Deckle (open source)

Product page: https://casavargas.app/deckle/ | Repo: https://github.com/CasaVargas/deckle | Case study: https://casavargas.app/work/deckle/

Deckle is the free, open-source desktop app for your e-ink reader. Its headline feature is the Deckle Daily: every morning it sets a real newspaper on your own computer, from your town's weather and news, your feeds and the articles you saved during the day, with a generated front page as the cover, and puts it on the reader. A Kindle gets it by USB or by Send-to-Kindle email; a Kobo gets a KEPUB and a PocketBook an EPUB the first time it is plugged in; a reMarkable 2, Paper Pro or Paper Pro Move gets a PDF laid out for its screen over its USB web interface; a Boox or an iPad gets each edition through an export folder (Dropbox, iCloud Drive), with color photos if wanted. Only Kindle books go through Amazon's free Kindle Previewer 4, which Deckle drives and never bundles; the other readers need nothing else. It also turns an EPUB you own into a Kindle book that reads like one bought from the store: drop the books on the window, plug in the Kindle, press Send. Runs on macOS 14 or later (Apple silicon and Intel) and Windows 11; Linux is unsupported for now. Built with Rust, Tauri and React. License: GPL-3.0-or-later. Status: pre-alpha, version 0.7.0 (many papers from one Mac, each with its own sections, schedule and days; a large-print layout; interests, topics searched every morning and kept only when a headline names them; papers you subscribe to on BLOX (TownNews) sites printed in full; ten masthead faces; several Kindles by name; DRM-free MOBI and AZW3 rebuilt as KFX; RTF, OpenDocument and FictionBook import; and a redesigned app). Earlier releases added Markdown and notes folders as books, three book styles, search across the library and Kindles, and an optional Daily AI editor that is off by default. Deckle also keeps every edition (the Morgue), reflows text PDFs, takes Word documents and text files, binds several files into one book, exports looked-up words to Anki, and writes each edition as a documented data bundle for reader apps. It also upgrades the DRM-free AZW3 and MOBI books already on a Kindle when it finds the originals in calibre or a folder, shows the Kindle's shelf, clears space, and backs up and restores its DRM-free books with their highlights. Verified on a Kindle Scribe (2024) over MTP and a Kindle Paperwhite over USB mass storage; other Kindles pending; Kobo, PocketBook and reMarkable are checked only against simulated devices so far. Windows installers are code-signed by Casa Vargas LLC. No account, no subscription, no telemetry; the app checks GitHub for a newer version at launch and installs nothing without a click. Kindle is a trademark of Amazon.com, Inc.; Kobo, PocketBook, reMarkable and Boox belong to their makers; Deckle is not affiliated with any of them.

Why it exists: sideloaded books on a Kindle miss Enhanced Typesetting, lose their covers, and get no page numbers, X-Ray or Word Wise. Each fix exists as a separate calibre plugin or forum recipe, and they conflict: the one that adds X-Ray removes the cover on a 2024 Kindle Scribe. Deckle does all of it in one tool and picks the trade-off per Kindle.

What it does:
- The Deckle Daily: a front page that is also the cover (the Kindle library tile is today's paper); sections in order with an index; whole stories with grayscale photos, Reader-View style, paywalled stories kept as headlines; weather from Open-Meteo, local news from a Google News search and local feeds, your RSS/Atom feeds, Your Reading (saved by bookmarklet, Inbox folder or iPhone Shortcut), a horoscope Deckle writes itself, On this day from Wikipedia, optional lottery numbers; scheduled each morning, delivered on plug-in or by email, newest three kept; no keys or accounts, and a failing source prints "unavailable today" while the paper still ships.
- Enhanced Typesetting through Kindle Previewer, repackaged as a monolithic KFX.
- Covers that stay: per Kindle, it sends a store-style book with its own cover thumbnail (Kindles that mount as a USB drive) or a personal document whose cover always shows (MTP-only Kindles such as the Scribe 2024, Colorsoft and Paperwhite 2024), unless the book matched a real Amazon edition.
- Approximate page numbers, X-Ray (people and terms, optional descriptions from an AI model the user chooses, including a local Ollama, or Wikipedia) and Word Wise (hints pointing at the Kindle's own English dictionary when present).
- Word documents, plain text, Markdown files and notes folders, text PDFs, web articles and finished KFX files through the same pipeline; several files can be bound into one book.
- A library of plain folders (Author/Title plus a JSON sidecar) and a Kindle tab showing what is on the device and which books can be rebuilt better.
- Every network use is listed in the README; all except a one-time 12 MB Word Wise dictionary download are off by default.

How it's built: Deckle's KFX writer is a Rust port of jhowell's kfxlib, tested byte for byte against kfxlib's output, so no Python ships. It carries its own small PTP/MTP client over USB for MTP-only Kindles (always the 32-bit ObjectInfo layout, because libmtp's layout switch makes Kindle writes fail with 0xA806). X-Ray is a SQLite sidecar in the schema WordDumb reverse-engineered. Word Wise is matched against Deckle's own Wiktionary-derived lexicon of 174,000 senses with per-book proper-noun detection. Every feature starts as a design document in the repository and is tested against fixtures and a simulated Kindle disk image.

On the record: GPL-3.0-or-later. First release 0.1.0 on 19 October 2026 for macOS, Windows and Linux. Verified on a Kindle Scribe (2024) over MTP: cover, X-Ray and Word Wise, and on a Kindle Paperwhite over USB mass storage. About 36,000 lines of Rust in 11 crates. Credits: jhowell (KFX Input/Output, kfxlib), jloutsch (kfxgen), xxyzz (WordDumb, Proficiency), seapy (kindle-cli), calibre's Kindle driver; Wiktionary via kaikki.org and wordfreq (CC BY-SA 4.0).

## In development

### Cathode TV
Product site: https://cathodetv.app | Case study: https://casavargas.app/work/cathode-tv/

Cathode TV is an IPTV player for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple TV and Vision Pro. It plays the playlists and program guides you already have. It is one SwiftUI codebase, with each platform built around its own input: touch, keyboard, the Siri Remote, or eyes and hands. It is in development and due in 2026, as a single purchase with no subscription.

Why it exists: an IPTV playlist is just a list of channels. The guide data that makes it watchable usually arrives as a large, compressed XML file that most players handle poorly, and on Apple TV especially, a player has to get focus, remote input and channel changes exactly right, or it feels broken however good it looks. Cathode TV treats the guide and the channel change as the core of the product, not as features.

What it does:
- Plays your own playlists. M3U and M3U8 playlists, the Xtream Codes API and XMLTV guides.
- A seven-day guide. Every channel gets a timeline that opens at the current time, with now and next, genre filters and the week ahead.
- Quick channel changes. A mini-guide overlay, gesture controls and picture in picture.
- A home screen from your guide. Rows for what's live now, tonight's highlights, live sports and movies starting soon.
- Programme details from TMDB. Posters, cast and ratings for guide programs and for your provider's on-demand library.
- Profiles that sync. Several profiles with parental controls, and favorites synced over iCloud.

How it's built: channel changes run on a time budget. The player swaps items rather than rebuilding the video layer, a small pool of warm players pre-buffers the channels you are likely to switch to next in the direction you have been switching, the stream format that worked last time is remembered per channel so the fallback sequence isn't repeated, and a signpost measures every change from tap to first frame. The guide parser streams a gzipped XMLTV file: it is decompressed to disk and read with a streaming parser that first checks the opening bytes to catch an HTML error page posing as a guide; programmes are sorted per channel, so "what's on now" is a binary search, and a compressed disk cache lets the app open without a network. On Apple TV, the player's on-screen controls run on a five-state machine that replaced four separate flags and their sixteen combinations, so only one element can hold focus at a time and the focus engine never has to choose; the guide grid never recycles the focused cell, and when it rebuilds it keeps you at the same time of day, not the same scroll offset. Channels live in SQLite with a full-text index for search, lists load in pages, and the Apple TV work was tested against a synthetic catalog of about 80,000 channels.

### Nimbus
Case study: https://casavargas.app/work/nimbus/

Nimbus is a Mac app for cloud storage. It lets you browse, copy, sync and mount remotes from S3, Google Drive, OneDrive, SFTP and the rest of rclone's long list. It doesn't reimplement any provider: it drives rclone and puts a native interface on top, including a Finder extension so your remotes show up where your files already are. Nimbus is in development. There is no release date yet.

Why it exists: rclone is the most capable cloud-storage engine there is, but using it means a terminal and a config file. The usual alternative is one vendor app per cloud, each with its own sync folder and its own idea of how a Mac should behave. Nimbus keeps rclone's reach and its open config format, and drops the command line.

What it does:
- Your remotes, in Finder. A File Provider extension lists your remotes in Finder. Files download when you open them, and edits go back up.
- Mount a remote as a volume. Mount any remote as a Finder volume. Mounts marked to open at launch, or left open when you quit, come back on the next launch.
- Add a remote without the config file. A guided sheet asks only the questions rclone needs for that provider, and providers that use OAuth sign in through your browser. Existing rclone configs import as they are.
- Browse, copy and sync. List and grid views with Quick Look and type-to-select; drag between clouds to copy; copy or sync any two remotes or folders, with progress in a Transfers view and the menu bar.

How it's built: the app and its Finder extension talk to the same local rclone process through RcloneKit, a typed Swift client for rclone's remote-control API. The engine's port is shared through the app group, and no provider is ever reimplemented in Swift. The rclone contract is tested, not assumed: four behaviors were checked against the real rclone and fixed, among them that listings return paths relative to the remote's root and that the API has no download call, so file contents come through rclone's own file server, with the lesson that a mock proves the client's shape, not the server's contract. Adding a remote walks rclone's own configuration flow instead of a hand-built form per provider, 13 questions for S3 instead of 78 options and 8 for Google Drive instead of 52, and a test pins those counts so an rclone upgrade that changes the flow fails loudly rather than silently. Deciding what to restore and which stale mounts to clean up are pure, unit-tested functions; leftover NFS servers from a crashed session are stopped before a new mount starts, and automatic remounting happens at most once per session. The build fails on hard-coded font sizes, which protects Dynamic Type, and on any remote Swift package dependency.

On the record: more than 50 providers, through rclone. About 200 test functions across the app and RcloneKit.

### AppPulse (working title)
Case study: https://casavargas.app/work/apppulse/

AppPulse finds the third-party apps on your Mac, checks for newer versions, and installs them after a chain of checks. The last check confirms the download was signed by the same developer as the app you already have. Every step is logged. There's no telemetry, no account and no sudo. AppPulse is in development. There is no release date yet.

Why it exists: a valid code signature only tells you that some registered developer signed a file. It doesn't tell you that the same developer made the app you're about to replace. An updater that trusts its metadata and then checks only the signature can be pointed at the wrong app, and many apps have no reliable update channel at all. AppPulse is built around being honest about both problems.

What it does:
- Updates from two sources. It reads Homebrew's cask data as plain data, without running brew to check, and Sparkle update feeds verified with EdDSA.
- Installs with rollback. The old app is cloned before the new one is swapped in, and any failure swaps it back.
- Says so when it can't compare. When two version schemes don't line up, it reports them as incomparable instead of guessing. Downgrades are shown, never applied.
- Shows its work. A summary of your library, a step-by-step install timeline, and a log of every decision it makes.
- Control per app. Skip, snooze, ignore or pin to a major version. Checks run on a schedule while it's open, and silent installs are opt-in behind a five-part gate.

How it's built: the first time AppPulse sees an app, it records the installed copy's Team ID and treats it as the pin. From then on, a different Team ID is a hard stop, whatever the metadata says, so the check still holds if every upstream source is wrong. Authenticated sources come first: Sparkle with EdDSA, then Homebrew's cask data, then Sparkle without a signature, because the EdDSA key already sits inside the installed app so a network attacker can't swap it, and cask data can't be the integrity anchor since some casks skip the checksum entirely. It never runs .pkg installers, whose scripts run as root. It never uses sudo, never replaces a running app, and never launches an app to see whether an update worked. A disk image that needs a license agreement becomes a download-only update. The core library can't import AppKit or touch the file system, network or processes outside its adapter layer, and a CI script fails the build if it tries. Every process call passes an argument array, never a shell string. The Hardened Runtime is on, with no entitlements.

On the record: 272 automated tests, 19 of them against real system tools. An integration test installs a real app update over a copy of the installed version, then rolls it back.
